=== page: choices/index.html
title: Choices — The Future of Case Management IT
description: The least conventional decisions in the design, what each is for, and what it costs.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Parameters
Choices
Choices
Several decisions here are not what a team would reach for by default. Each one below says what it buys and what it costs, so you can disagree with it in particular rather than in general.
01 Store dated claims, not facts –
Why it is unusual
Most case systems store the current value of a field and log changes separately.
What it is for
Whether a person owes money back turns on whether the ministry knew something and failed to act. A current value with a change log beside it cannot answer that. The log sits outside the decision path.
What it costs
Every read gets harder. Developers have to think in periods rather than values, and every report has to say which point in time it means.
02 Track two kinds of time, and inherit a third +
Why it is unusual
Finance has modelled two kinds of time for decades. Case management almost never does.
What it is for
A tribunal asks two questions: what was true, and what did the ministry know. Each needs its own axis. The third axis exists because fifteen years of records arrive from a system still in use. Flatten their history into the migration date and a whole class of question stops having an answer.
What it costs
More storage, and a real learning curve. Most inherited records will not know their third date, and the system has to say so rather than guess.
03 Five case models rather than one +
Why it is unusual
The conventional move is a single configurable case model shared across programs.
What it is for
A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal share almost nothing. A shared model turns every change into a negotiation. The last programme cut scope rather than reopen one.
What it costs
The plumbing gets written five times. That is a real cost, and the design accepts it on purpose.
04 Decisions read no live data +
Why it is unusual
Teams usually call the rules engine as a service, and it fetches what it needs while it runs.
What it is for
A decision that reads anything not stored with it cannot be re-run. Re-running is what lets you show a tribunal what happened, rather than piece it together from memory.
What it costs
Someone has to gather the facts before the decision runs, and gathering them consistently is a problem of its own.
05 The interface outlives its implementation +
Why it is unusual
Teams normally treat the translation layer over a legacy system as the lasting asset.
What it is for
Replacing a system in pieces only works if nobody calling it can tell which piece answered. The published interface is permanent. The translation layer behind it is temporary, and its team answers for winding itself up.
What it costs
The published interface has to refuse old vocabulary, even on the days when exposing it would be faster.
06 Store the letter, not just the decision +
Why it is unusual
Most systems treat letters as output rather than as part of the record.
What it is for
A tribunal asks what the person was told as often as it asks what the system worked out. A decision that re-runs perfectly, next to a letter nobody can rebuild, still misses the question.
What it costs
Template versions and content hashes have to survive as long as the decisions that point at them.
07 Retention lives on the type, not the storage location +
Why it is unusual
Most systems work out how long to keep something from where it sits.
What it is for
Guessing from location fails the first time a fact appears in two places, which is day one. Attach the classification and the retention rule to the kind of evidence instead. Then destroying records becomes a job you can actually do.
What it costs
Every evidence type needs a records ruling before anyone can use it, which puts the records office on the critical path.
How the design was arrived at
This architecture rests on every document we could recover about ICM and the work it supports. Each claim traces back to a primary source, or the documents confirm it between themselves, or the arithmetic gives it. Claims we could not check say so on the page.
The design began with the assumptions that ICM rested on, and much of the approach to MIS with it. We tested eleven. None came through intact. Two of them:
System residency is a legal requirement
No federal or provincial statute says government systems have to sit in Canada. No published policy says it either.
Worries about data sovereignty and trade still point to keeping the systems in Canada, and the architecture does that. No formal guidance stands behind the choice.
Replacing the existing system has a deadline
The vendor has committed to support the current platform to at least December 2037, on a rolling ten-year basis.
Nothing outside the programme forces the replacement to finish by a set date. So it can do discovery, research and analysis properly before it commits to building at scale. An unforced timetable takes a great deal of risk out of the work.
Two of the eleven assumptions that did not survive testing.
What the evidence base is
Two bodies of source material sit behind this. The first is 57 technical design documents for the current release. They cover the application, its integrations, its data conversion and its reporting. The second is 326 service-delivery procedures, describing how the work gets done.
Reading both matters, because they disagree about what the system is. The technical documents describe 61 applications. The procedures turn up 28 more tools that a worker touches and no technical document mentions. Among them: a standalone calculator, a reporting tool, credit and asset-check portals, a worker-safety device, a vital statistics service.
What remains unresolved
The architecture carries 40 open items to verify, and 30 more to settle before the design freezes. Three are worth naming here, because they change the shape of the work rather than its detail:
Whether the rules can move off the mainframe on their own, given that both of them calculate.
Whether we can settle what the third time axis holds before the first production record lands. Nobody can add it afterwards.
What service levels the analytical platform can promise. That waits on a storage benchmark nobody has run yet.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
Figures on this site are drawn from the architecture document and from 326 service-delivery procedures. Nothing here is a government commitment.

Current State
This design does not set out to contradict the current system. It comes from one question. Why does a large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of capable and well-meaning people, still fail the organizations it serves? The answer lies in what the system leaves out: what it ignores, and what it pushes outside itself.
What the SDPR procedures are
Every recurring task a caseworker does has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as staff really deliver it.
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it carries out, the law behind it, and how the system classifies the work. That turns the whole set into a map of the services.
326procedures
15capability areas
128kinds of work request
84statutory provisions cited
146distinct forms
13ways to reach the ministry
Work crosses system boundaries constantly
63% of documented procedures need two or more systems to finish one task.
Number of procedures by count of separate systems required, across 326 procedures.
Systems
Procedures
Proportion
0
39
1
80
2
114
3
51
4+
42
Highlighted rows are the 207 procedures that cross a system boundary. Four procedures require seven.
Counted by naming every system referenced in each procedure. The most common pairing is the Siebel case system with the client portal, then the case system with Service Canada, then the case system with the mainframe.
One journey, three systems, two re-keys
Recovering an overpayment is the clearest example. A worker who has decided someone was paid too much has to:
Open a separate web application to calculate the amount. It does not connect to either system of record.
Print the result, scan it, and attach it back to the case.
Move the case file to their own office in the mainframe so they have permission to act on it.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Move the case file back to where it came from.
Clients whose earnings are annualised need one step more: a spreadsheet. The worker reads figures off one screen, types them into the sheet, and types the result back.
None of this is anyone's poor practice. The procedure says to do it this way, because with the systems that exist this is the right way.
Where the rules actually live
A modernisation has to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement sit in four separate places, and only one of them is a rules engine.
Business rules by location
Where
What it holds
A rules engine
29 separate rulebases covering eligibility, validation, debt and payment calculation
The mainframe
Benefit calculation, rate recalculation, time limits, sanction end dates
Formulas inside the case system
Retention periods, access levels, privacy calculations
A database table
The rates the public-facing eligibility estimator uses
Found by reading the technical design documents for the current release alongside the procedures. Nothing on record gives the 29 rulebases source control, a promotion pipeline or a version register.
Routing runs on a spreadsheet
An Excel workbook decides which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes. Fifty-six procedures point at it. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. So the priorities and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, kept up by hand.
Accommodation and the signature problem
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have little access to a computer. A worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
That path skips portal registration, so the applicant never gets a personal identification number. The electronic signature depends on that number. So the people the accommodation exists for are the people who then cannot sign electronically.
How these figures were produced
The counts come from reading the Resource Finder and the other document stores in full, then pattern-matching and mapping the text. Named systems, capability areas and the policy behind each procedure come from the documents and the policy manual.
Nobody has measured the volumes yet. You can count caseload throughput, worker streams, transaction rates and queue depth directly. The figures here come from the technical design documents instead.
The rest of the site sets out how the design answers these conditions. Start with evidence. The overpayment journey above follows directly from a record that cannot say what the ministry knew, or when.

=== page: determinations/index.html
title: Determinations — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why an entitlement decision is treated as a function that can be re-run years later.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Parameters
Choices
Determinations
Someone can challenge a decision about their entitlement years after the ministry made it. So the design treats every decision as something you re-run, not something you remember.
The problem with asking a system what it decided
Ask a typical case management system why a person got a particular amount in March 2022 and it will work the sum again. It uses today's rules, today's data and today's software, then reports the answer with confidence. The answer may well be right. Nobody can tell, and nobody can show a tribunal the difference.
Three things have shifted underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, perhaps several times. And someone upgraded the software. A rules engine upgrade can change how the same rule reads, and nobody notices until a client appeals.
Treating a decision as a function
The design makes entitlement a calculation with no hidden inputs. It reads the rules, the facts and the date it is deciding for. While it runs it does not read the clock, query a database, or call another service. It gets everything it needs up front.
That rule sounds academic. It is what makes the next part work: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
The function signature
Determine(rulesArtefactVersion, evidenceSnapshot, referenceDate) → DeterminationResult
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine gives you this on its own. The shell around the engine enforces it. The engine runs in-process against a snapshot passed by value, and that is what puts byte-identical replay within reach rather than in the brochure.
Five things stored with every decision
Storing the answer is not enough. Storing the answer and the rules is still not enough. The system binds five artefacts into the record at the moment it makes the decision.
1 The rules Content digest, tagged and immutable once released Stored
2 The engine Version number and the archived binary Stored
3 The facts it saw Copied in full into the record, never referenced Stored
4 The reasoning Which rules fired and which branches were taken, in a ministry-owned format Stored
5 The letter Content-hashed template, resolved at decision time Stored
The decision can be replayed.
Four years on, the same inputs produce the same answer, the reasoning can be read aloud, and the letter the client received can be reproduced.
Switch any artefact off to see which question stops being answerable. Each one covers a failure the other four do not.
Teams leave out the fifth one most often. A decision that reproduces perfectly, next to a letter nobody can rebuild, still misses the question the tribunal asked. That question is often about what the person was told, not about what the system worked out.
How long replay has to work
Archiving the software tells you what it was. It does not promise that anything in twenty years can still run it. The operating system, the processor and the container runtime all die younger than a child protection record, which the ministry keeps for ninety years.
Rather than leave that hanging, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Years 0–7
We archive the software itself and test it every quarter to confirm it still runs. Seven years covers the appeal, reconsideration and audit paths that really do re-run a decision.
Years 7–20
The rules live on as a written specification, with a test suite that any rebuild has to pass. The suite stays independent of the engine from day one, so this handover costs nothing when it comes.
Beyond 20 years
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record. Re-running stops being on offer. This is what a paper file has always been.
The three stages run in order, which is why they are numbered. The last one holds up because the ministry declared it in advance, rather than discovering it during a hearing.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Storing the inputs makes replay reliable. It says nothing about whether the inputs were gathered consistently. That is where the remaining gap sits.
Gathering the facts means reading across several stores that update on their own schedules. Two decisions issued seconds apart, with one store briefly behind, can each see a different world quite legitimately. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far catches it. So the design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events. A later reader can then tell which view of the world a decision was made against.
Decisions that affect people carry their own classification
Every rule carries a label saying what kind of decision it produces. Some produce an administrative decision, which needs reasons. Some produce a decision a person has to make before it takes effect. The rest are working sums that affect nobody on their own.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. A decision that goes against someone sends out its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it, because the label says it must. Not because somebody remembered.

=== page: domains/index.html
title: Domains — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the design uses sixteen separate models rather than one, and the rules that keep them separate.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Parameters
Choices
Domains
Perhaps the biggest choice in this design is where to draw the lines between parts of the system. Twelve domain models, one of which is really five sub-domains, which makes sixteen.
The problem of a single model
Programmes like this usually start by building one model of a case that every program can share. That is how MIS began, and how ICM began. It looks like the responsible choice: less duplication, one place to change things, one way of working across the ministry.
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Make them share a lifecycle and every change to one has to be negotiated with everyone else. Multiply that over dozens of programs and nobody can change the model at all. So teams bolt on sub-entities, extend them, and add more ways to integrate. The system turns into a plate of spaghetti. You cannot change anything in one place, and any failure reaches everywhere. This is not hypothetical. ICM merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope for exactly this reason.
This design takes the difference seriously. Five program families get five case models. The plumbing is written more than once, and that is cheaper than the alternative.
What the parts are
Shared spine
Participant Identity
Evidence & Verification
Eligibility & Entitlement
One per program family
Employment assistance
Child protection
Child care subsidy
Employment services
Persons with disabilities
Money
Payments & Issuance
Financial Components
Overpayment & Recovery
Delivery
Appeals & Reconsideration
Work Management
Documents & Capture
Notices & Correspondence
Provider & Outcome
Evidence & Verification
Every dated claim about the world, and how it was checked.
Owns
The evidence succession set, verification policy, the four operations, three time axes.
Does not own
It does not decide anything. It records what was claimed and what was verified.
Boundary test
Its events are the trigger fabric for everything else.
Select any part to see what it owns, what it deliberately does not own, and the test that tells you when the boundary has been breached. The five case models share protocols, not a case model.
Four rules keep the lines in place
A boundary that lives only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These four are written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
Each part can be released on its own
It has its own storage and its own message topics. If two parts always ship together, they are one part wearing two names.
No part reads another part's database
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This rule erodes first, and takes the longest to notice.
There are exactly two ways to talk
A published interface for reads, and published events for notices. There is no third way, and adding one is not a shortcut.
Copies are owned by whoever holds them
A part that needs another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events and shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
The thin identity model
Participant Identity stays deliberately small. It holds identifiers, enough detail to tell two people apart, and whether anyone has proven the identity. No addresses, no income, no relationships.
This part is the most likely to drift, because every new requirement brings a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model is back, in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
Merge and split go in on day one rather than later. The audit of the previous system found duplicate records at scale, and called its search ineffective and exact-match only. Adding merge afterwards to a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible. By then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would hold still.
Published events and the boundary test
Participant Identity publishes PersonRegistered, IdentityMerged, IdentitySplit, IdentifierAdded and IdentifierInvalidated. Every other context keeps its own projection (Payee, Applicant, Caregiver, Reporter, Appellant, Debtor), keyed by participant identifier.
Evidence & Verification publishes EvidenceRecorded, EvidenceActivated, EvidenceSuperseded, EvidenceVerified, EvidenceInvalidated and EvidenceCorrectionRecorded.
Parts that are not domain models
Some pieces are shared infrastructure rather than parts of the business. Platform teams own them and everyone uses them. The difference matters. A platform part that starts holding program state has quietly become a seventeenth domain model, and nobody chartered it.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters point in opposite directions on purpose. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive whatever implements it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it answers for winding itself up.
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.

=== page: evidence/index.html
title: Evidence — The Future of Case Management IT
description: Why the system records dated claims rather than facts, and why it tracks two kinds of time.
Skip to content
[aria-label] The Future of Case Management IT — overview
The Future of Case Management IT
Menu
[aria-label] Sections
Overview
Current State
Evidence
Domains
Determinations
Parameters
Choices
Evidence
ICM tracks facts. It overwrites fields and buries history. In the new system the unit of information is a dated claim, tied to its evidence and to whoever made it. Later work can disprove that claim, confirm it, overturn it or replace it, and nothing is lost on the way.
Why not store facts?
A system that stores only the current state, "Income: $900", leaves the important questions open. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number, or the number we recorded at the time?
Front-line staff adapt, so the information is not lost. It is just not modelled. It goes into notes, forms and attachments, and only a thin slice of it is ever held as data.
This is not an auditing nicety. It closes the gap between how the system holds data and how front-line staff work. Substantiating evidence against claims is the most common task a worker performs, and the system does not model it at all, so it is done by hand. Social workers spend hours mapping their notes onto a structure that serves the software rather than their clients.
So the unit of storage is an assertion:
what household composition: couple
about whomparticipant 4471-A
true forfrom 1 January, open-ended
learned on12 September
fromeligibility review finding
verifiedtenancy agreement, 14 September
One evidence assertion, from a case where the dates are in dispute. The ministry now says the household was a couple from January. It reached that view in September. In between it paid eight months at the single rate. Which of those two dates you read decides what happens next.
The four things that can happen to an assertion
Once the system records something, nobody edits it in place. Four operations change what the system believes. They differ in one respect: what each does to the period the claim covers.
[aria-label] Evidence operations
Record
Supersede
Correct
Invalidate
The world changed.
valid time
a new period
transaction time
now
The earlier assertion stays true for its own period. The new one takes over from a later date.
For example A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
If this produced an overpayment, the classification rule reads the operation as the world having changed.
Select an operation. Supersede and Correct both replace an earlier claim, but only Correct says the earlier claim was wrong about its own period. That is what separates a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.
That distinction is why the model exists. It is a policy rule written into the shape of the data. It applies consistently because the record itself names the operation that caused the recalculation. Nobody has to guess at it afterwards.
The operation feeds the classification without settling it. Who caused the error matters too. A client who hid a relationship is not in the same position as a worker who mis-keyed a figure. The model promises something narrower and more useful: the question has an answer at all, and the answer comes from the record rather than from whoever opens the file today.
Where a conventional record gives up
Take the assertion above to a tribunal. The client accepts a relationship exists but disputes that it began in January. Three separate things are now in question, and they are easy to confuse:
What the ministry believed about the household in each of those eight months.
When the ministry changed its mind, and on what evidence.
What start date the ministry now asserts.
A conventional design holds one relationship start date, plus an audit entry saying a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot touch the first. It leaves the eight monthly payments looking like errors. Each one was the right answer to what the ministry knew at the time.
The operations, formally
Operation
Valid time
Transaction time
Meaning
RecordEvidence
asserted period
now
We learned a new fact
SupersedeEvidence
new period
now
The world changed
CorrectEvidence
same period
now
We were wrong about the world
InvalidateEvidence
closed
now
The assertion should never have existed
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The third date, and the history problem
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
Old records all arrive on the same day. Make that migration date the "when we learned it" date and every historical fact looks as though it arrived at the same moment. Supersede and Correct then look identical across the whole pre-cutover record. The overpayment rule stops working on exactly the records where most overpayments sit.
The third axis holds the date the old system asserted the fact, where the old record still shows it. Often it cannot be read at all, so the date carries a confidence marker. Where the answer is unknown, the system says so rather than guessing.
valid time
The period in the world for which the fact holds.
Set by whoever asserts it, from the source.
transaction time
When this system learned it.
Set at recording. Never changes.
legacy assertion time
When the previous system asserted it, if that can be decoded.
Set at migration. Often unknown, and marked as such.
Three dates on every assertion. The third can be empty, and the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than swapping in the migration date.
Nobody can add this later. Events are immutable: you can introduce a field with a default, but you cannot fill it in afterwards. Either the migration decoded the source or it did not. So the decision has to come before the first production record.
Confidence values and replay behaviour
legacy_asserted_at travels with legacy_assertion_confidence, which takes DECODED (read straight from the legacy record or audit trail), INFERRED (worked out from a related artefact by a written rule) or UNKNOWN.
On UNKNOWN, any consumer working out a knowledge-state answer must return INDETERMINATE. That covers the overpayment rule, a tribunal reconstruction view and a disclosure history. Projections that answer only valid-time questions ignore the field.
Backdated recalculation runs off valid time, which any competent migration preserves, so recalculation survives. Something narrower breaks without the third axis: what the ministry knew and when. That is the question separating a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.

A PWD* designation granted in July.
It takes effect from March.
Four months of payments were right when the ministry made them. They are now an underpayment: four months a client went without money they turn out to have been owed. The current system keeps only today's answer. It rewrites history instead of recording it. What did we know, when did we know it, and how do we prove it? This design keeps all three.

Asked in Jun about May, the system reports a monthly entitlement of $1,060.
Current version of the record: At application in March, no disability designation is in place.
Today the system reports $1,535.50 for May. The payment actually made that month was correct when it was issued, and is now an underpayment of $475.50.
Move either slider. The left one changes the month you ask about. The right one changes the month you ask in. The hard edge across the grid is the July decision reaching back over every earlier month. That is what a backdated decision looks like when the system keeps both axes.
Current State
Two ministries run case management: Children and Family Development, and Social Development and Poverty Reduction. The work covers assistance payments, service requests, social work, loss recovery and client support. All of it depends on a worker seeing the full picture. The work is life-critical. A wrong answer means someone might not eat this month, or a child misses a check-in.
Two systems do the work. One is an Oracle Siebel customer relationship management product, adapted for government. The other is a mainframe built in 1982. They run side by side and share the core programs between them. Every attempt to retire the mainframe has stalled or failed.
The New Design is Built on Three Pillars
Evidence, not 'facts'
The system will not store "this person is an adult." It stores this: on 14 July, AI agent ID-33422 read the uploaded image of identification, matched it to the case, and read the date of birth as 22 April 1988. Business rules then decide the person is an adult. Who or what decided, when, and on what basis all sit in the record. They do not sit in an attached PDF, or outside the system altogether.
Evidence
Apt boundaries
Two ministries with broad mandates carry a very mixed portfolio. The current system forces all of it into one rigid model. That is how a design turns brittle. Here each program family gets its own model.
Domains
A decision you can re-run
Every entitlement decision stores the rules, the engine, the facts it saw, its own reasoning and what it decided. A manager four days later, or a tribunal years later, can re-run it instead of piecing it together from memory.
Determinations
Why do backdates matter?
Much of case management is building one clear timeline as information arrives. It does not arrive in order, and what turns up later can change what earlier events meant. In the backdated designation above, the client spent four months short of what they were owed. Someone on assistance has no savings to absorb that. The same machinery runs the other way too. It lands on the same person, who then has to pay the money back.
When someone is paid too much, the money falls into one of two classes. If the client's circumstances changed and they told the ministry late, it is a recoverable overpayment. The ministry takes it back at $10 a month, out of a payment that was already only just enough. If the ministry held the information all along and did not act on it, that is administrative error, and the client should not carry it.
Telling those two apart means knowing when the ministry knew. That is a transaction-time question. A system that records only when a fact was true cannot answer it. Nor can one that stamps every moved record with the date it moved. Almost the whole overpayment backlog sits in records from before any cutover.
Mispayment is one example of many. Evidence has to back nearly every claim a client makes. That cycle of claim, evidence and proof is the core loop of the whole service.
How this is modelled
Every evidence assertion carries three time dimensions: valid_time (the period in the world for which the fact holds), recorded_at (when this system learned it), and legacy_asserted_at (when the old system asserted it, where the old record still shows that).
The third axis is nullable. It carries a confidence value of DECODED, INFERRED or UNKNOWN. On UNKNOWN, any consumer working out a knowledge-state answer must return INDETERMINATE. It must not quietly substitute the migration timestamp.
None of this can be added later. Events are immutable: you can add a field with a default, but you cannot fill it in afterwards. The axis has to exist before the first production event.
What this site covers
These pages set out the domain model, and the thinking behind the least conventional choices. Each one leads in plain English and keeps the technical statement behind a disclosure.
Read Current State first if you do not know ICM and MIS. The design makes most sense against what it replaces. Parameters lists the twenty-one rules the design has to hold to, each with the check that catches a breach.
DRAFT
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
Figures on this site are drawn from the architecture document and from 326 service-delivery procedures. Nothing here is a government commitment.

Parameters
Twenty-one rules the design has to hold to. Each one is written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies. Six of them cannot be added once the work has started.
What a parameter is
A parameter is something a compliant system does, stated with the check that catches its absence. It is not a promise and not a hope. The wording shows the difference: every entry below ends in a question you can put to a running system and get a wrong answer to.
The architecture states twelve. Testing them turned up three faults. Two said the same thing in different words. Two carried two ideas each, and you could drop either idea without touching the other. And one gap, which the architecture names in its own text, was nobody's job. The set below fixes each of those and adds seven more rules on top.
The set makes three claims. Every parameter is necessary: take one away and the design loses something nothing else supplies. No two overlap: nothing is said twice. And together they carry what the architecture is trying to do. Each entry below demonstrates the first two claims. The third rests on an argument against a list of intents, and it is the weakest of the three, because another architect could reasonably draw some of these lines elsewhere.
The set

N07
The calculation reads nothing but its inputs
No clock, no database, no service calls inside the decision. It gets everything it needs up front. The record it writes comes out of the decision, and never feeds back into it.
Why it cannot be dropped
Purity is what makes an identical re-run possible in practice rather than on paper. A rules service that fetches what it needs ties every decision to a running system. That is the first thing a tribunal will probe.
The test that fails
Feed it the same rules, the same engine version and the same inputs. Does it produce a byte-identical trace? Does it touch the clock, the environment or any service on the way?
Where it came from
From P8, narrowed to the calculation
Cannot be added later
The engine must be sealed before the first rule is written
Grouped by the axis each one sits on. Select any parameter to see the check that catches a breach. A heavy left edge marks the six you cannot add later.
Six cannot be added later
You can satisfy most of these late, at a price. Six you cannot. Each one has to be in place before a particular first event. Once that event has happened, the fix is a rebuild rather than a repair.
Before the first rule is written N07
The engine is sealed off from live data. A rule authored against a service it can call has already fixed the shape of every rule after it.
Before the first event is written N12, and the third date in N01
How records are destroyed is decided per class of fact. Events are immutable, so a date can be added with a default but never filled in afterwards.
As the first copy is made N06, N21
Where a copy came from, and what its source bars it from, are written at the moment of copying. Neither can be reconstructed later.
From the first decision N09
The point in the event sequence a decision read from goes into its record. Earlier decisions cannot be tied to a consistent view of the world.
Before the first group of clients moves N14
Moving them back is proven rather than claimed, and what the return trip loses is written down and approved.
The gates in the order delivery reaches them. This says what order the work has to happen in. It does not say which rules matter most.
Do first only what cannot be done later.
Where the twenty-one came from
Every principle in the architecture is accounted for. Seven carried across, with their wording narrowed or widened. Three split, because each held two ideas that could stand apart. One took in a clause from another, and one became more general. So twelve principles turned into fourteen parameters, and seven more joined them.
P1 split N01 · N02
P2 narrowed N08
P3 split N03 · N06
P4 absorbs P3(a) N03
P5 carried N04
P6 extended N11
P7 carried N10
P8 narrowed N07
P9 carried N05
P10 generalised N18
P11 split N12 · N13
P12 carried N14
Added N09 · N15 · N16 · N17 · N19 · N20 · N21
N09 closes a gap the architecture names in its own text. N15 and N16 close two more it had already recorded against itself. The last four came out of the policy manual, which turned out to state rules the architecture had never reached.
Those last four are the interesting ones, because nobody found them by thinking harder about the architecture. They came from reading what the ministry already tells its own staff to do. Policy sets time limits, and missing one changes what a client is owed. It names which entitlements a client can appeal, and to whom. It keeps the person who decides apart from the person who reviews. And it bars certain uses of information the ministry may lawfully hold. The twelve could not express any of that.
A rule nobody can check is not a rule
One parameter is not about the system at all. N18 ranges over the other twenty. It makes each of them name how you catch a breach, and it says that anything you could write as a lint rule or a compatibility check has to be written as one.
It stands on its own rather than folded into the others. File a rule about enforcement among the rules about behaviour, and enforcement stops being anybody's job without anyone deciding that it should.
What the set does not settle
Three things are open, and they are recorded rather than smoothed over.
Continuity has no footing in policy
N16 asks for recovery targets per service, proven by exercise. We mapped 270 policy obligations, and not one of them exercises it. A benefits platform plainly needs recovery targets, so that does not show the rule is unnecessary. It shows that its authority sits somewhere other than the policy manual. Until someone names that source, the rule stays proposed rather than baselined.
Whether to build this at all
N11 says you buy generic capability, and that someone other than the builder checks any decision to build. At component level the architecture answers the question, though each component's own owner gives the answer. At platform level it does not answer it at all. Nowhere in the source's 4,998 lines does anyone weigh a custom build against a commercial case management product. By the architecture's own rule that is a compliance failure rather than a matter of taste, and it is the largest open question on this page.
The premise underneath the decision model
Everything on the determinations page rests on one premise: that you can express an entitlement decision as a function of recorded evidence. Review conceded the premise may be false for some decisions. It drives roughly 28% of programme cost, and it appears in no assumption register. It belongs in one.
What the set is checked against
The sufficiency argument runs against a numbered register of what the architecture is trying to achieve. An intent with no parameter behind it means the set is not sufficient. A parameter carrying no intent means it was not necessary.

Four places where the set could have been drawn differently. They are recorded here so that reopening one is a deliberate act rather than a rediscovery.
N01 and N02. The architecture bundles these as one principle with one test. A reviewer who thinks the rule on payloads follows from the model of a fact would merge them, giving twenty.
N12 and N13. The split turns on custodianship having a different authority and a different rights holder from disposition. An architect who treats Indigenous jurisdiction as one input to a single records design would keep them together.
N09. Arguably a clause of N08 rather than a parameter of its own. It stands apart because N08's test cannot detect its breach, and nobody enforces a clause its parent's test cannot see.
N15. Merges accessibility and digital exclusion, because they fail the same way. An architect who treats them as separate obligations would split it.
Four parameters do most of the work on the rest of this site: N01 on evidence, N03 on domains, and N07 to N09 on determinations. The choices page sets out what several of them cost.

A boundary that lives only in a diagram will not survive delivery pressure. These four are written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies.
A breach is visible rather than professed
A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal share almost nothing. A shared model turns every change into a negotiation. The last programme cut scope rather than reopen one.
A client is told the truth about what they may challenge
A conventional design holds one relationship start date, plus an audit entry saying a worker changed it on 12 September. That answers the third question, gestures at the second, and cannot touch the first. It leaves the eight monthly payments looking like errors. Each one was the right answer to what the ministry knew at the time.
A database table
A decision is defensible at tribunal four years later
A decision stores which rules version ran against which evidence version. It stores the artefacts themselves rather than pointing at them. It also records what the client asked for, which criteria they met and which they did not, what the ministry assumed, what evidence was missing, and the date the client heard.
A decision that reads anything not stored with it cannot be re-run. Re-running is what lets you show a tribunal what happened, rather than piece it together from memory.
A decision you can re-run
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, covering employment assistance, disability assistance, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection.
A design proposal for the successor to British Columbia's integrated case management systems, explained in plain English.
A document is not evidence.
A document is what a verification policy accepts as satisfying an evidence type. Losing that distinction turns the file store into a second system of record.
A fact is a dated claim with a source
A first assertion about a period nothing covered yet.
A modernisation has to know what it is replacing. The rules that decide entitlement sit in four separate places, and only one of them is a rules engine.
A parameter is something a compliant system does, stated with the check that catches its absence. It is not a promise and not a hope. The wording shows the difference: every entry below ends in a question you can put to a running system and get a wrong answer to.
A part that copies evidence records where it came from. When the source corrects it, you can list everyone holding a copy, and each of them has to act. That holds even where a decision already went out on the old value.
A part that needs another's data keeps its own copy, built from that part's events and shaped the way it needs. When the source corrects something, the copy has to follow.
A partner moves in on 1 May, and the client reports it.
A person can reach the same outcome whatever their disability and whichever route they take. Interfaces meet the Province’s accessibility standard at first release, and every journey has a supported route that is not digital.
A pointer resolves to whatever the database says today. Replay returns today’s answer to a four-year-old question.
A pointer to a running system is not evidence. Replay has to outlive everything that produced the decision, the engine included. The client is also owed the record itself, put together and severed under FOIPPA. Replay alone does not deliver that.
A published interface for reads, and published events for notices. There is no third way, and adding one is not a shortcut.
A review establishes the household was a couple from January, not a single person.
A rule nobody can check is not a rule
A rules engine
A shared model decides whose release everyone else waits for. The previous programme merged its last two phases and cut child protection scope because of exactly this.
A store with no disposition design cannot acquire one afterwards
A system that stores only the current state, "Income: $900", leaves the important questions open. How do we know? What evidence is there? When did we know? Is this the corrected number, or the number we recorded at the time?
A team accountable for a thing will grow and protect it. A team measured on its own dissolution will not.
A tribunal asks equally what the client was told.
A tribunal asks two questions: what was true, and what did the ministry know. Each needs its own axis. The third axis exists because fifteen years of records arrive from a system still in use. Flatten their history into the migration date and a whole class of question stops having an answer.
A tribunal asks what the person was told as often as it asks what the system worked out. A decision that re-runs perfectly, next to a letter nobody can rebuild, still misses the question.
Accommodation and the signature problem
Accounts, accruals, schedules, double-entry postings.
Added since the source
All twenty-one
An Excel workbook decides which queue a request joins, how urgent it is, how long it has, and where a scanned document goes. Fifty-six procedures point at it. One of its sheets maps 445 form numbers to their handling. So the priorities and service-level targets for the whole service sit outside the platform, kept up by hand.
An append-only store and a legal duty to destroy pull against each other. Settle that after the first event and you are rebuilding, not repairing. The timing is the rule: a correct design that arrives late has failed.
An engine upgrade can change how the same rules evaluate.
An entitlement determined twice must not be paid twice, and that guarantee lives here rather than in five case contexts.
Appeals & Reconsideration
Apt boundaries
Archiving the software tells you what it was. It does not promise that anything in twenty years can still run it. The operating system, the processor and the container runtime all die younger than a child protection record, which the ministry keeps for ninety years.
Arguably a clause of N08 rather than a parameter of its own. It stands apart because N08's test cannot detect its breach, and nobody enforces a clause its parent's test cannot see.
As the first copy is made
Ask a typical case management system why a person got a particular amount in March 2022 and it will work the sum again. It uses today's rules, today's data and today's software, then reports the answer with confidence. The answer may well be right. Nobody can tell, and nobody can show a tribunal the difference.
Ask about
Asked in
At application in March, no disability designation is in place.
At application, the client declares they live alone.
Backdated recalculation runs off valid time, which any competent migration preserves, so recalculation survives. Something narrower breaks without the third axis: what the ministry knew and when. That is the question separating a recoverable debt from the ministry's own error.

Before the first event, has someone chosen the mechanism for each class of fact and published what survives?

Benefit calculation, rate recalculation, time limits, sanction end dates
Beyond 20 years
Boundaries and authority
Boundary test
Business rules by location
Buy, adopt or reuse the common parts: workflow, notification, identity, secrets, policy evaluation, scheduling, document storage, search, print and mail. To build one instead, name a legal, policy or programme need that no off-the-shelf option meets. Someone other than the component’s owner has to agree. Wanting it faster does not count.
Can a reviewer tell from the schema which product implements it? Then remove the product and count the changes to the contract.
Can this group return to the old system today, without a data project, and can you name every class of fact that would not survive the trip? Correction-versus-supersession has no destination in the old system: if that is not on the list, the list is incomplete.
Can you replay a decision made three years ago from storage alone, with nothing running? Can you put together the appeal record and sever it on demand?

Capture, attachment lifecycle, extraction, e-signature, and the link between a document and the claim it supports.

Continuity and control
Continuity has no footing in policy
Copied in full into the record, never referenced
Copies are owned by whoever holds them
Copying creates this duty, and nothing else discharges it. A design that passes nothing on at all still passes every boundary rule perfectly. It also leaves people paid on a value we know to be wrong.
Correct a fact at its source. Can you list every part holding a copy? Does each one have to act? And does anything raise an alarm when a correction goes unread?

Counted by naming every system referenced in each procedure. The most common pairing is the Siebel case system with the client portal, then the case system with Service Canada, then the case system with the mainframe.

Current State — The Future of Case Management IT
Current version of the record:
Custodianship is modelled, not assumed
Cuts a reviewer could reasonably reopen
Decide how records end, per class of fact, before anything is written. A schedule, an indirection, or destroying one person’s key. Publish what survives a destruction, design who holds the keys, and say what a replay does when it meets an event it cannot read.
Decide outside the legislated time and eligibility runs from the date the decision was due, not the date it came. So a missed deadline changes what the client is owed. An unmodelled clock is a source of wrong entitlement, not a service-level gap.

Documents & Capture
Does any part read another part’s tables, or depend on a type it does not own? The second question catches the failure that really happens. Shared models come back as schemas, not as databases.
Does not own
Does the bar sit on the information rather than in a procedure? Does it survive a copy into another part? Does a read that fails to state its purpose get refused? And does a blocked use leave an event behind?
Does the design name the watermark, write it into the decision record, and hold it to a stated limit? Does a decision outside that limit fail rather than go ahead?
Does the model hold each limit once, with its owner, its class, its start event, duration, extensions and authorisations? Does a breach show up without a person spotting it, and does its consequence apply automatically?
Domains — The Future of Case Management IT
Each one carries a header naming its purpose, the policy it carries out, the law behind it, and how the system classifies the work. That turns the whole set into a map of the services.
Each parameter names how you catch a breach of it. Anything you could write as a lint rule, a fitness function or a compatibility check gets written as one.
Each part can be released on its own
Each part keeps its own picture of a person, a case, a payment. No canonical Person, no shared schema, no join across parts, no dependency on a type another part owns.
Effort concentrates on what is distinctive to the ministry

Employment assistance
Employment services
Every copy is traceable, and every correction reaches it
Every dated claim about the world, and how it was checked.
Every entitlement decision stores the rules, the engine, the facts it saw, its own reasoning and what it decided. A manager four days later, or a tribunal years later, can re-run it instead of piecing it together from memory.
Every evidence assertion carries three time dimensions:
Every evidence type needs a records ruling before anyone can use it, which puts the records office on the critical path.
Every principle in the architecture is accounted for. Seven carried across, with their wording narrowed or widened. Three split, because each held two ideas that could stand apart. One took in a clause from another, and one became more general. So twelve principles turned into fourteen parameters, and seven more joined them.
Every read gets harder. Developers have to think in periods rather than values, and every report has to say which point in time it means.
Every recurring task a caseworker does has a written procedure: what starts it, which screens to open, which form to send, what to type in which field. Together they run to 8.2 million characters. They describe the service as staff really deliver it.
Every rule carries a label saying what kind of decision it produces. Some produce an administrative decision, which needs reasons. Some produce a decision a person has to make before it takes effect. The rest are working sums that affect nobody on their own.
Every rule carries a way of catching a breach
Every service carries an availability target and stated recovery times, set against what its failure does to a client. An exercise has to demonstrate them. Shared infrastructure takes the strictest target of anything that depends on it.

Finance has modelled two kinds of time for decades. Case management almost never does.
Financial Components
Five case models rather than one
Five things stored with every decision
For any evidence type, can you name its custodian? Does the system read that, or do people just follow a convention? And does every access decision trace back to the agreement registry, and to nothing else?
For each entitlement the system records four things: the law it rests on, whether a decision can go to reconsideration, whether it can go to appeal, and to which body. It records them per entitlement and per variant. It never takes them from the parent programme.
For each journey, can a person finish it on every supported channel? Does the outcome change with the route? For each interface, has someone tested it with assistive technology, and not just run a scan? A scan catches around 30% of issues.
For each parameter, name the check and say whether it runs automatically. Where a person checks something a machine could check, say which one, and why nobody has automated it.
For every custom-built component, name the legal, policy or programme need that no off-the-shelf option meets. Then name who agreed, other than the builder.
For every entitlement and every variant, can the system state the law it rests on, whether it goes to reconsideration, whether it goes to appeal, and to which forum? And can it do that without borrowing any of it from the parent?
For every entitlement, name who decides and who reviews, and say what the ministry keeps for itself. Does every decision trace back to the person who reasoned it, as opposed to anyone who advised?
For every record in transition, name the one system of record and the group it covers. If the answer is “it depends on the field”, someone has split the work across fields instead of across groups of clients.
For example
Formulas inside the case system
Found by reading the technical design documents for the current release alongside the procedures. Nothing on record gives the 29 rulebases source control, a promotion pipeline or a version register.
Four months of payments were right when the ministry made them. They are now an underpayment: four months a client went without money they turn out to have been owed. The current system keeps only today's answer. It rewrites history instead of recording it. What did we know, when did we know it, and how do we prove it? This design keeps all three.
Four or more
Four parameters do most of the work on the rest of this site: N01 on
Four places where the set could have been drawn differently. They are recorded here so that reopening one is a deliberate act rather than a rediscovery.

From the first decision
Front-line staff adapt, so the information is not
Gathering the facts means reading across several stores that update on their own schedules. Two decisions issued seconds apart, with one store briefly behind, can each see a different world quite legitimately. Both replay perfectly. Both are reproducible. They disagree, and nothing described so far catches it. So the design pins each snapshot to a point in the sequence of recorded events. A later reader can then tell which view of the world a decision was made against.
Gathering the facts means reading stores that update on their own schedules. So the decision records the point in the event sequence it read from. It sets a limit on how far behind a store may be, and refuses to issue outside that limit.

It does not disburse.
It has its own storage and its own message topics. If two parts always ship together, they are one part wearing two names.

Limits on use travel with the information
Merge and split go in on day one rather than later. The audit of the previous system found duplicate records at scale, and called its search ineffective and exact-match only. Adding merge afterwards to a system that assumed one person equals one row is close to impossible. By then every payment instruction and every stored decision has keyed itself to an identifier the design promised would hold still.
Merges accessibility and digital exclusion, because they fail the same way. An architect who treats them as separate obligations would split it.
Mispayment is one example of many. Evidence has to back nearly every claim a client makes. That cycle of claim, evidence and proof is the core loop of the whole service.
Modelled once, not per program family. An allowed appeal is a retroactive determination, not a manual adjustment.

Much of case management is building one clear timeline as information arrives. It does not arrive in order, and what turns up later can change what earlier events meant. In the backdated designation above, the client spent four months short of what they were owed. Someone on assistance has no savings to absorb that. The same machinery runs the other way too. It lands on the same person, who then has to pay the money back.

N09 closes a gap the architecture names in its own text. N15 and N16 close two more it had already recorded against itself. The last four came out of the policy manual, which turned out to state rules the architecture had never reached.
N09 · N15 · N16 · N17 · N19 · N20 · N21
N11 says you buy generic capability, and that someone other than the builder checks any decision to build. At component level the architecture answers the question, though each component's own owner gives the answer. At platform level it does not answer it at all. Nowhere in the source's 4,998 lines does anyone weigh a custom build against a commercial case management product. By the architecture's own rule that is a compliance failure rather than a matter of taste, and it is the largest open question on this page.

N12, and the third date in N01
N16 asks for recovery targets per service, proven by exercise. We mapped 270 policy obligations, and not one of them exercises it. A benefits platform plainly needs recovery targets, so that does not show the rule is unnecessary. It shows that its authority sits somewhere other than the policy manual. Until someone names that source, the rule stays proposed rather than baselined.

New, from the gaps the architecture records
New, from the gaps the architecture records; still proposed
No addresses, no payment details, no employment records, no relationships. Those are evidence, owned elsewhere.
No clock, no database, no service calls inside the decision. It gets everything it needs up front. The record it writes comes out of the decision, and never feeds back into it.
No federal or provincial statute says government systems have to sit in Canada. No published policy says it either.
No part depends on a model it does not own
No part reads another part's database
No shared tables. No joins across schemas. Not for a report, and not in a test environment. This rule erodes first, and takes the longest to notice.
No system named
Nobody can add this later. Events are immutable: you can introduce a field with a default, but you cannot fill it in afterwards. Either the migration decoded the source or it did not. So the decision has to come before the first production record.
Nobody can explain the decision in words. It can perhaps be re-run, but it cannot be accounted for.
Nobody can reason about logic spread across layers, test it, or change it with confidence. You end up unable to say which copy is the authoritative one. Keeping it together also makes validation uniform: no integration or migration script can slip past a rule the data itself enforces.
Nobody has measured the volumes yet. You can count caseload throughput, worker streams, transaction rates and queue depth directly. The figures here come from the technical design documents instead.
None of this can be added later. Events are immutable: you can add a field with a default, but you cannot fill it in afterwards. The axis has to exist before the first production event.
None of this is anyone's poor practice. The procedure says to do it this way, because with the systems that exist this is the right way.
Nothing else catches a lawfully held fact reaching a use it was barred from. Policy bars five different things: an attribute, a class of content, a counterparty, a subject matter, and an act of communication. Only the first has anything to do with a calculation.
Nothing else catches a missing recovery duty. Every recovery figure in the architecture covers the analytics platform. None covers the published interface, the translation layer, the decision service or the case stores. Bringing the system back does not put a missed payment run right.
Nothing else in the set catches a system that is correct, reproducible, well-bounded, and out of reach of the people it exists for. Usage totals hide that failure completely, and it falls on clients and front-line staff.
Nothing else says who may exercise an authority. The decision record names what was decided and by whom. It does nothing to stop one person deciding, reviewing and releasing the money. Policy states all three limbs directly.
Nothing is stored as a bare value. Every fact carries who claimed it, the period it covers, the date this system learned it, and the date the old system asserted it, or a marker saying that date cannot be read.
Nothing on this site is a government commitment, and none of it is a record of any real person.
Nothing outside the programme forces the replacement to finish by a set date. So it can do discovery, research and analysis properly before it commits to building at scale. An unforced timetable takes a great deal of risk out of the work.

One authoritative implementation per rule
One evidence assertion, from a case where the dates are in dispute. The ministry now says the household was a couple from January. It reached that view in September. In between it paid eight months at the single rate. Which of those two dates you read decides what happens next.

Published events and the boundary test
Published interfaces use policy and domain words, not the vocabulary of whatever product sits behind them. The interface is the permanent artefact; the translation layer over the existing system is temporary, and its team is chartered to disband.
Pure: no clock, no database, no service calls.
Pure: no input or output, no clock reads, no database access, no service calls. No rules engine gives you this on its own. The shell around the engine enforces it. The engine runs in-process against a snapshot passed by value, and that is what puts byte-identical replay within reach rather than in the brochure.
Purity is what makes an identical re-run possible in practice rather than on paper. A rules service that fetches what it needs ties every decision to a running system. That is the first thing a tribunal will probe.
Rather than leave that hanging, the design commits to a horizon in three stages and writes it down in advance.
Reach does not depend on the client’s capability or channel

Take the assertion above to a tribunal. The client accepts a relationship exists but disputes that it began in January. Three separate things are now in question, and they are easy to confuse:
Tasks, assignment, caseload balancing, supervisory queues, overdue surfacing, escalation.
Teams leave out the fifth one most often. A decision that reproduces perfectly, next to a letter nobody can rebuild, still misses the question the tribunal asked. That question is often about what the person was told, not about what the system worked out.
Teams normally treat the translation layer over a legacy system as the lasting asset.
Teams usually call the rules engine as a service, and it fetches what it needs while it runs.

Template lifecycle, content hashing, rendering, channel selection, proof of what was sent.
Template versions and content hashes have to survive as long as the decisions that point at them.
That distinction is why the model exists. It is a policy rule written into the shape of the data. It applies consistently because the record itself names the operation that caused the recalculation. Nobody has to guess at it afterwards.
That label travels with the decision into the letter. A decision that goes against someone sends out its reasons, its appeal period and the route to challenge it, because the label says it must. Not because somebody remembered.
That path skips portal registration, so the applicant never gets a personal identification number. The electronic signature depends on that number. So the people the accommodation exists for are the people who then cannot sign electronically.
That rule sounds academic. It is what makes the next part work: if nothing hidden went in, then storing what went in is enough to reproduce what came out.
The Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act commits the Province to alignment. A Nation’s governance over its own data will not fit into a retention rule or an access list. A PDF agreement cannot grant an access right, and nobody can audit a right that came from somewhere else.

The New Design is Built on Three Pillars
The aggregate is the evidence succession set: the stream of versions of one logical fact about one subject. Commands append events; current state is a projection. Verification status transitions are themselves events.
The architecture bundles these as one principle with one test. A reviewer who thinks the rule on payloads follows from the model of a fact would merge them, giving twenty.
The architecture carries 40 open items to verify, and 30 more to settle before the design freezes. Three are worth naming here, because they change the shape of the work rather than its detail:
The architecture names the hole in its own text. Two decisions issued moments apart, with one store briefly behind, can each see a different world quite legitimately. Both replay. Both reproduce. They disagree, and nothing else notices.
The architecture states twelve. Testing them turned up three faults. Two said the same thing in different words. Two carried two ideas each, and you could drop either idea without touching the other. And one gap, which the architecture names in its own text, was nobody's job. The set below fixes each of those and adds seven more rules on top.

The set
The set makes three claims. Every parameter is necessary: take one away and the design loses something nothing else supplies. No two overlap: nothing is said twice. And together they carry what the architecture is trying to do. Each entry below demonstrates the first two claims. The third rests on an argument against a list of intents, and it is the weakest of the three, because another architect could reasonably draw some of these lines elsewhere.
The shape of the payload is what carries provenance across the line. A row arrives with no sign of who claimed it. So the receiver cannot know what it may conclude, and a later correction has nothing to attach to.
The smallest rule surface, which is why it is captured first.
The snapshot names the moment it was read
The split turns on custodianship having a different authority and a different rights holder from disposition. An architect who treats Indigenous jurisdiction as one input to a single records design would keep them together.
The stored reasoning, the letter and the facts are the record. Re-running stops being on offer. This is what a paper file has always been.
The sufficiency argument runs against a numbered register of what the architecture is trying to achieve. An intent with no parameter behind it means the set is not sufficient. A parameter carrying no intent means it was not necessary.

There are exactly two ways to talk
There is a path for applicants who need an interpreter, find reading difficult, or have little access to a computer. A worker reads the questions aloud and enters the answers for them.
These pages set out the domain model, and the thinking behind the least conventional choices. Each one leads in plain English and keeps the technical statement behind a disclosure.
This architecture rests on every document we could recover about ICM and the work it supports. Each claim traces back to a primary source, or the documents confirm it between themselves, or the arithmetic gives it. Claims we could not check say so on the page.
This design does not set out to contradict the current system. It comes from one question. Why does a large, expensive piece of software, laboured over by hundreds of capable and well-meaning people, still fail the organizations it serves? The answer lies in what the system leaves out: what it ignores, and what it pushes outside itself.
This design takes the difference seriously. Five program families get five case models. The plumbing is written more than once, and that is cheaper than the alternative.
This is an internal working draft. Sign in with your government account to read it.
This is not an auditing nicety. It closes the gap between how the system holds data and how front-line staff work. Substantiating evidence against claims is the most common task a worker performs, and the system does not model it at all, so it is done by hand. Social workers spend hours mapping their notes onto a structure that serves the software rather than their clients.
This is what a decision-maker reads out at a hearing.
This is what makes replacement in pieces possible at all. The interface published today over the old platform is the one published tomorrow over the new services. Confuse the contract with the layer and you bind old vocabulary to the new architecture. That is the failure the programme exists to reverse.
This part is the most likely to drift, because every new requirement brings a reason to add one more field to the person record. Once that starts, the shared model is back, in the one place the design most needs to stay thin.
Those last four are the interesting ones, because nobody found them by thinking harder about the architecture. They came from reading what the ministry already tells its own staff to do. Policy sets time limits, and missing one changes what a client is owed. It names which entitlements a client can appeal, and to whom. It keeps the person who decides apart from the person who reviews. And it bars certain uses of information the ministry may lawfully hold. The twelve could not express any of that.
Three dates on every assertion. The third can be empty, and the design treats an unknown value as unknown rather than swapping in the migration date.
Three systems
Three things are open, and they are recorded rather than smoothed over.
Three things have shifted underneath since March 2022. Policy changed. The person's recorded circumstances changed, perhaps several times. And someone upgraded the software. A rules engine upgrade can change how the same rule reads, and nobody notices until a client appeals.
Time spent building common capability is time not spent on decisions that reproduce, and that is where the programme will be judged. Without an outside check the test marks its own homework, which is how it fails today.
To see how one business rule works, how many systems do you have to open? If more than one, say which is authoritative, why the others exist, and what generates them.
Today the system reports
Track two kinds of time, and inherit a third
Transaction time
Treating a decision as a function
Twenty-one rules the design has to hold to. Each one is written so a reviewer can point at something and say whether it complies. Six of them cannot be added once the work has started.
Two bodies of source material sit behind this. The first is 57 technical design documents for the current release. They cover the application, its integrations, its data conversion and its reporting. The second is 326 service-delivery procedures, describing how the work gets done.
Two decisions made moments apart can disagree
Two ministries run case management: Children and Family Development, and Social Development and Poverty Reduction. The work covers assistance payments, service requests, social work, loss recovery and client support. All of it depends on a worker seeing the full picture. The work is life-critical. A wrong answer means someone might not eat this month, or a child misses a check-in.
Two ministries with broad mandates carry a very mixed portfolio. The current system forces all of it into one rigid model. That is how a design turns brittle. Here each program family gets its own model.
Two of the eleven assumptions that did not survive testing.
Two of them are worth naming, because their charters point in opposite directions on purpose. The published interface is permanent: it is the contract built to outlive whatever implements it. The translation layer over the existing Siebel system is temporary, and the team that builds it answers for winding itself up.
Two systems
Two systems do the work. One is an Oracle Siebel customer relationship management product, adapted for government. The other is a mainframe built in 1982. They run side by side and share the core programs between them. Every attempt to retire the mainframe has stalled or failed.
Two time axes are standard. This design carries a third, because the new system inherits fifteen years of records from systems that are still running.
Type the amount into the mainframe by hand.
Valid time
Version number and the archived binary
We archive the software itself and test it every quarter to confirm it still runs. Seven years covers the appeal, reconsideration and audit paths that really do re-run a decision.

What 326 service-delivery procedures show about how the work is actually done.
What a parameter is
What happens next is well documented. A child protection investigation and a child care subsidy renewal have almost nothing in common beyond involving a person. Make them share a lifecycle and every change to one has to be negotiated with everyone else. Multiply that over dozens of programs and nobody can change the model at all. So teams bolt on sub-entities, extend them, and add more ways to integrate. The system turns into a plate of spaghetti. You cannot change anything in one place, and any failure reaches everywhere. This is not hypothetical. ICM merged its final two phases and cut child protection scope for exactly this reason.

What this site covers
Whatever holds the data enforces its own rules. Logic is not split between the data, a configuration table and an unwritten process.
When someone is paid too much, the money falls into one of two classes. If the client's circumstances changed and they told the ministry late, it is a recoverable overpayment. The ministry takes it back at $10 a month, out of a payment that was already only just enough. If the ministry held the information all along and did not act on it, that is administrative error, and the client should not carry it.

Whose record it is is an attribute the system reads. The model covers the non-Crown participant class properly rather than approximating it. Handing a record to another sovereign is one of the ways it can end. And sharing agreements are machine-readable artefacts that grant the access rights themselves.

Why not store facts?
Why the design uses sixteen separate models rather than one, and the rules that keep them separate.
Why the system records dated claims rather than facts, and why it tracks two kinds of time.
Without it, nothing downstream can be rebuilt. You cannot replay a decision against evidence when nobody knows what period it covered. And you cannot tell a correction apart from a change in the world.

Work items reference identifiers. They never carry copies of evidence.
Worries about data sovereignty and trade still point to keeping the systems in Canada, and the architecture does that. No formal guidance stands behind the choice.

You can move any group of clients back without a data project, and an approved statement says what the return trip loses. Reversibility covers both the mechanism and how much survives.

page rests on one premise: that you can express an entitlement decision as a function of recorded evidence. Review conceded the premise may be false for some decisions. It drives roughly 28% of programme cost, and it appears in no assumption register. It belongs in one.
